svg.aria-label: Basic forging operations: 1 Drawing out: draw out wrought iron and mild steel at orange-yellow (about 1000-1100°C), working over the rounded edge of the anvil so the metal only moves lengthwise; turn the work 90° after every blow to keep the section square, as hammering from one direction only gives a diamond section; work from the root to the end a section at a time. 2 Upsetting: heat only the part to be upset (about 2-3 times the diameter long) and dip the rest in water to keep it hard; stand the work upright on the anvil face, hot end up, and hammer straight down on the end; if it starts to bend, straighten it at once or it folds into a crack; upset no more than about 3 times the diameter. 3 Bending: heat only the part to bend; bend curves over the anvil horn or a round bar and right angles over the square edge of the anvil; the outside of the bend stretches thin, so for a strong right angle upset the corner a little first; afterwards tap it true on the flat anvil face. 4 Punching: heat to orange-yellow to yellow, hotter than ordinary forging; punch about 2/3 of the thickness, turn over and punch at the darker spot on the back, with the work over the anvil hole or an iron ring, to drive out the slug; pull the punch out every few blows to dip it in water and sprinkle a pinch of charcoal powder in the hole; punching right through from one side gives a crooked hole and a ragged burr on the back. 5 Hot cutting: cut while red hot, with a soft iron or copper plate under the work, never straight on the anvil face; cut about halfway in with the hot chisel, turn over, line up with the cut and cut again, and when only a thin skin is left lay it on the anvil edge and snap it off with light blows; to cut thin stock cold, chisel a deep groove with a cold chisel and snap it; the end flies off, so nobody stands in front. 6 Each heat: bury the work just above the centre of the fire and turn it to heat through; on taking it out brush off loose scale; shape with heavy blows first, lighter as it darkens, and put it back in the fire at blood red; a small piece gives only 20-40 seconds of work per heat; one job per heat. Fire colours: dark red about 500-550°C, light straightening only; blood red about 650-700°C, where wrought iron and mild steel go back in the fire; cherry red about 780-850°C, the lower limit for forging high-carbon steel, which goes back in the fire at cherry red; bright red about 850-950°C; orange-yellow about 1000-1100°C, the best forging heat; yellow about 1200°C; bright yellow to white about 1250-1300°C, for forge welding only. Wrought iron and mild steel forge best at orange-yellow to yellow; high-carbon steel is forged only between cherry red and orange-yellow. Never hit hard once it stops glowing; mild steel at about 200-400°C, with a blue oxide colour on the surface, is especially brittle. Wear goggles; tong jaws must fit the work
